title: Improve Mathematical Reasoning in Language Models by Automated Process Supervision
data_curation: Uses the MATH dataset (Hendrycks 2021) with the PRM800K train/test split: 12K training questions and a 500-problem MATH500 holdout. OmegaPRM runs MCTS with a search limit of 100 per question, yielding 15M raw per-step annotations that are down-sampled to 1.5M for PRM training -- claimed as the largest such dataset to date. To reduce false-positive/false-negative noise from Monte Carlo estimation, questions are filtered by running k=32 rollouts and discarding those with no correct answer (too hard) or no wrong answer (too easy). Step segmentation is flexible: any consecutive token span is a valid step, targeting ~16 pieces per solution rather than rule-based newline splitting. Baselines are PRM800K (human) and Math-Shepherd (auto). Generator policies are instruction-tuned Gemini Pro (~51% MATH) and pretrained Gemma2 27B (4-shot).
curriculum: Not a focus of this paper. The pipeline is a single data-then-inference loop rather than a staged training curriculum: instruction-tune (or 4-shot prompt) a policy, collect OmegaPRM annotations via MCTS, train a PRM from a pretrained checkpoint with a pointwise soft-label classification objective, then apply the PRM only at inference time through weighted self-consistency over sampled solutions. No RL fine-tuning, preference stage, or warmup/anneal schedule is applied to the generator.
method: OmegaPRM is a divide-and-conquer MCTS algorithm (inspired by AlphaGo Zero) that automates process-supervision data collection. Two key ideas: (1) binary-search Monte Carlo -- split a candidate solution at its midpoint and run k=8 rollouts; if any rollout reaches the gold answer the prefix is correct (error lies after), else the error lies before, recursing in O(k log M) instead of O(kM). (2) MCTS over a state-action tree reuses all rollouts: Select picks a rollout via a PUCT-style rule with Q(s,r)=alpha^(1-MC(s)) * beta^(len(r)/L) (alpha=0.5, beta=0.9, L=500, c_puct=0.125), favoring 'supposed-to-be-correct wrong-answer' rollouts; Binary Search locates the first error and adds new edges; Maintain updates N, MC, Q. The PRM is trained with pointwise soft-label BCE (y_hat=MC(s)), pointwise hard label, or a Bradley-Terry pairwise loss; soft label wins. Inference uses PRM-weighted majority voting (product of step scores).
eval_metrics: Evaluates on MATH500 and GSM8K using PRM-weighted majority voting (% problems solved) at k=64 (and accuracy-vs-sample curves). Baselines: majority vote, +Math-Shepherd, +Math-Shepherd (own impl), +PRM800K, +OmegaPRM. Headline: instruction-tuned Gemini Pro rises 51%->69.4% on MATH500 and 86.4%->93.6% on GSM8K; Gemma2 27B rises 42.3%->58.2% on MATH500 and 74.0%->92.2% on GSM8K. A separate PRM step-classification accuracy test favors pointwise soft label (70.1%) over hard (63.3%) and pairwise (64.2%). Efficiency: at equal compute OmegaPRM yields 15M points vs 200K for brute-force Monte Carlo, a 75x speedup.
key_results: Gemini Pro: 51%->69.4% on MATH500 and 86.4%->93.6% on GSM8K; Gemma2 27B: 42.3%->58.2% on MATH500 and 74.0%->92.2% on GSM8K, all via OmegaPRM-weighted majority voting. 1.5M auto-annotations collected at 75x the efficiency of brute-force Monte Carlo.
evolution_note: Builds on PRM800K's human process supervision and Math-Shepherd/MiPS's per-step Monte Carlo automation, importing AlphaGo Zero's MCTS to make step-level reward data cheap and large-scale. As a 2024 PRM-data contribution it predates and motivates the later wave of process-reward-model and RLVR work that needs abundant automated step-level credit assignment.
